cards.front: Mitral stenosis is most commonly due to [chronic rheumatic heart] disease
cards.raw0: Mitral stenosis is most commonly due to {{c1::chronic rheumatic heart}} disease
cards.back: - Rheumatic fever is rare in developed countries; however, it is the most common cause of mitral stenosis worldwide - Left atrial enlargement due to MS predisposes to atrial fibrillation and thromboembolic complications (e.g., stroke) - Hemoptysis is due to erosion of the bronchial arteries

cards.front: Chronic mitral stenosis may result in left [atrial] dilatation due to volume overload
cards.raw0: Chronic mitral stenosis may result in left {{c1::atrial}} dilatation due to volume overload

cards.front: One possible complication of mitral stenosis is [atrial fibrillation] with associated risk for mural thrombi
cards.raw0: One possible complication of mitral stenosis is {{c1::atrial fibrillation}} with associated risk for mural thrombi
cards.back: - Secondary to left atrial dilatation due to volume overload - Atrial fibrillation in the setting of MS carries an even higher thrombogenic risk than nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, and routine anticoagulation with warfarin is indicated regardless of CHA 2 DS 2 -Vasc score - Valvular atrial fibrillation = Afib with moderate to severe mitral stenosis OR with mechanical heart valve - Non-valvular atrial fibrillation = Afib with any other valvular heart disease OR without valvular heart disease

cards.back: - Blood cultures should be obtained before initiating antibiotic therapy or obtaining cardiac imaging in patients with suspected infective endocarditis - Transthoracic echo (TTE) is the best initial test for all patients - Transesophageal echo (TEE) is for select patients due to higher sensitivity (high-risk features, inconclusive TTE, intracardiac complications) [img]

cards.front: The SA node is commonly supplied by the [ right coronary ] artery The AV node is commonly supplied by the [ dominant (right) coronary ] artery

  • The AV node is commonly supplied by the {{c1::dominant (right) coronary}} artery
cards.back: Supply of AV node: - Left dominant (5-10%) = left circumflex artery - Right dominant (70-80%) = right coronary artery - Infarct may cause nodal dysfunction (bradycardia, heart block) - In RCA infarct, ischemia causes damaged tissue to depolarize, and because the vagus nerve is close, it is stimulated causing vagus nerve suppression of AV node

cards.raw0: Enlargement of the heart can cause {{c1::hoarseness}} due to compression of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve

cards.raw0: One complication associated with lung cancer is {{c1::superior vena cava::vascular}} syndrome due to compression of the {{c1::superior vena cava (SVC)}}
cards.back: - Most commonly due to mediastinal masses (thymoma / mediastinal lymphadenopathy), less commonly due to right upper lobe lung / superior sulcus tumors - Patients will present with headache, dizziness, dyspnea, JVD, and position-dependent facial edema [img]

cards.front: Superior vena cava (SVC) syndrome is characterized by impaired drainage of the upper extremities , resulting in [edema] and dilated collateral veins in the [upper torso]
cards.raw0: Superior vena cava (SVC) syndrome is characterized by impaired drainage of the upper extremities, resulting in {{c1::edema}} and dilated collateral veins in the {{c2::upper torso}}
cards.back: - Blood is trapped in venous circulation leaving less blood to go through pulmonary circulation → shortness of breath - Increased pressure in the SVC vein causes blood flow to get rerouted through collaterals which become engorged and dilate, trapping blood in the venous system Collaterals include: - Internal (mammary) thoracic vein (where anterior intercostal veins drain with back up resulting in the blanchableness of anterior chest) - Lateral thoracic vein - Esophageal veins - Azygos vein (blood is rerouted through azygos to drain into IVC ) [img] Photo credit: EMAHKempny, CC BY-SA 4.0 , via Wikimedia Commons [img]

cards.front: Superior vena cava (SVC) syndrome is characterized by impaired drainage of the head & neck , resulting in [facial plethora] and [jugular venous distension]
cards.raw0: Superior vena cava (SVC) syndrome is characterized by impaired drainage of the head & neck, resulting in {{c2::facial plethora}} and {{c1::jugular venous distension}}
cards.back: - Fluid build-up in the head is dangerous because it can lead to cerebral edema → ischemia → Cushing reflex - Fluid build-up in the neck is dangerous because it can compress the trachea, larynx, and esophagus [img]

cards.front: SVC syndrome can be caused by [ thromboemboli ] from indwelling central venous catheters
cards.raw0: SVC syndrome can be caused by {{c1::thromboemboli}} from indwelling central venous catheters
cards.back: SVC syndrome is a medical emergency; indwelling catheters also often lead to thrombosis of subclavian or axillary vein [img]

cards.raw0: SVC syndrome can raise {{c1::intracranial}} pressure (if obstruction is severe), leading to headaches and dizziness
cards.back: - Also causes increased risk of aneurysm/rupture of intracranial arteries - This can also lead to retinal hemorrhage and stroke [img]

cards.raw0: Patients with large pericardial effusion have an enlarged "{{c1::water bottle}}" shaped heart on chest x-ray
cards.back: - May be associated with nonspecific symptoms such as dyspnea and fatigue (subacute) or cardiac tamponade (acute) - Notably, clear lungs on CXR [img] Photo credit: James Heilman, MD , CC BY-SA 3.0 , via Wikimedia Commons

cards.front: Subclavian steal syndrome typically occurs due to hemodynamically significant stenosis of the [subclavian] artery proximal to the origin of the [vertebral] artery
cards.raw0: Subclavian steal syndrome typically occurs due to hemodynamically significant stenosis of the {{c1::subclavian}} artery proximal to the origin of the {{c1::vertebral}} artery
cards.back: - Lowered distal subclavian arterial pressure leads to a reversal in blood flow ("steal") from the contralateral vertebral artery to the ipsilateral vertebral artery (resulting in vertebrobasilar insufficiency ) - Can also occur at the brachiocephalic trunk - Can have significant difference in brachial systolic BP between affected and unaffected arms (>15 mmHg) [img] Photo credit: Hellerhoff , CC BY-SA 3.0 , via Wikimedia Commons [img] [img]

cards.front: On a CT of the thorax , the [trachea] is a good landmark to localize the esophagus (located posteriorly) and the great vessels (located anteriorly)

cards.back: Radiolucency of air in the trachea demarcates it very well; esophagus is between trachea and the vertebral bodies [img] Photo credit: Mikael Häggström , CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

cards.front: Approximately 90% of left atrial thrombi are found within the [ left atrial appendage ] in patients with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation
cards.raw0: Approximately 90% of left atrial thrombi are found within the {{c1::left atrial appendage}} in patients with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation
cards.back: This is a small sac-like structure in the left atrium that is particularly susceptible to thrombus formation; these clots can then systemically embolize and cause a stroke - Valvular atrial fibrillation = Afib with moderate to severe mitral stenosis OR with mechanical heart valve - Non-valvular atrial fibrillation = Afib with any other valvular heart disease OR without valvular heart disease Left atrial appendage: [img] Right atrial appendage: [img] Image(s) provided by www.radiologyassistant.nl .
